en: Abhidhānottaratantra, Chapter 19 [Tibetan & Sanskrit, 22] = Lokesh Chandra facsimile edition = 1138 AD palm-leaf manuscript.
[89, beginning of folio] Now, for the sake of the arising of the welfare of all sentient beings, I shall describe the meditation upon this very one:
oneself instantaneously appearing as the goddess Pratyaṅgirā in her ritual form.
Four-faced and sixteen-armed, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture with a trampling stance,
she causes various wicked obstacles to fall down beneath her lotus seat.
Situated in the center of a lunar disc, she has faces that are white, blue, reddish-brown, and yellow.
Adorned with all ornaments,
beautified by white garments,
wearing a crown of the five Buddhas, she is the supreme reviver of the dead.
She has three eyes and a peaceful countenance, while others have fierce and terrifying faces; they hold a raised vajra and a threatening forefinger, as well as a bell, a noose,
and other implements, along with a thunderbolt, sword, trident, axe, skull-cup, and goad.
Another [form] holds a bow and a khaṭvāṅga, with her two ears filled;
she holds a mallet and a wheel, bestows fearlessness, and grants all accomplishments.
Alternatively, there is an eight-faced form on the left and right sides.
On the right, there is the blue-red, the yellow, and the fierce face with a laugh of "ha ha";
on the left, the green-red and likewise the smoke-colored;
above, the peaceful, very white, and moon-pale faces born of the body.
In the heart of this very [deity], situated in the center of a moon-maṇḍala,
one should recite with devotion and concentration the *Mṛtasañjīvana* mantra:
Oṃ amṛtasañjīvani + + + + + kh+ [= mahāmṛtamukhi] jīvaṃ praveśaya 2 sarvavajrapadma((samā))yoge mahābodhicittaviṭapitamūrte hūṃ 2 a ā aṃ aḥ svāhā || [89]
By this recitation, however, one who has died is restored to life in every way;

it pacifies untimely death and certainly causes the dead to rise. Then those most wonderful yoginīs, being well-pleased, danced while performing their rites, making sounds of "hīḥ hāḥ" and, being satisfied, crying out with shouts of "hā hā."
[... destroying with the sound *hai hai*, filling with the sound *hūṃ hūṃ*,

taking hold of the object of focus with the sound *hūṃ hūṃ*, slaying with the sound *phaṭ phaṭ*, impaling with the sound *hūṃ hūṃ*, drawing forth with the sound *jaḥ jaḥ*, honoring with the sound *saḥ saḥ*, proceeding well and with a beautiful voice, and subduing Māra with the sound *hūṃ bhrūṃ*.
The jambhinīs [are purified] by the syllable *hūṃ*.

With the syllable *hoḥ* they are full of passion; with the syllable *haṃ haṃ* they protect; with the syllable *phuḥ phuḥ* they satisfy; with the syllable *ḍāṃ* they nourish; with the syllable *ghraṃ ṭhaṃ* they possess flowers;
with the syllable *gaṃ gaṃ* they possess fragrance; and with the syllable *raṃ raṃ* they possess color.
It should be performed according to this procedure, in the proper sequence, namely, by means of the rites for pacification and so forth.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Meditation on the Revival of the Dead, the Performer of All Actions," from the *Abhidhānottarottara*.

[897'] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while traveling through the southern region, beheld five hundred merchantmen who had set out upon the great ocean to gather wealth. At that time, a fierce and violent wind arose, and they were driven by the force of the wind into the mouth of a sea monster. Seeing this, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara extended his right hand from Mount Potalaka and reached out to touch the heads of those merchants. By the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s majestic spiritual authority, the sea monster was unable to swallow them; instead, it released them back into the open ocean. Having been freed from the sea monster’s mouth, the merchants returned safely to Jambudvīpa. Those merchants then offered incense, flowers, and various kinds of music to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, and having paid homage to him, they departed. Subsequently, the merchants went to the place where the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One Śākyamuni resided, and having arrived there, they prostrated at the feet of the Buddha and sat to one side. Seated thus, the merchants addressed the Buddha, saying: “Blessed One, we were traveling through the southern region when we encountered a fierce and violent wind that drove us into the mouth of a sea monster. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara extended his right hand from Mount Potalaka and touched our heads. By the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s majestic spiritual authority, the sea monster was unable to swallow us and released us back into the open ocean. We have now returned safely to Jambudvīpa. When the Blessed One heard these words, he told the monks: “Monks, if you wish to see the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, you should all go together to Mount Potalaka. Then the monks, desiring to see the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, set out for Mount Potalaka. Upon their arrival, they saw the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara seated upon a lion throne made of seven precious substances, surrounded by a retinue of a hundred thousand bodhisattvas. Having seen him, they prostrated at his feet and sat to one side. Seated thus, the monks addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: “Noble son, we have come here wishing to see you. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied to the monks: “Venerable ones, if you wish to see me, you must first cultivate the roots of virtue and purify your minds. The monks asked: “What are the roots of virtue? The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied: “Venerable ones, the roots of virtue are as follows: first, one should take refuge in the Three Jewels; second, one should observe the precepts purely; third, one should practice generosity; fourth, one should cultivate loving-kindness and compassion; fifth, one should not harbor anger toward sentient beings; sixth, one should not engage in idle chatter; seventh, one should not be stingy with the Dharma; eighth, one should not disparage others; ninth, one should not be jealous of the merits of others; tenth, one should not be arrogant toward others. Venerable ones, if you can practice these ten roots of virtue, you will be able to see me. Hearing these words, the monks cultivated the roots of virtue and purified their minds. After some time, they again went to Mount Potalaka to see the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Upon their arrival, they saw the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara seated upon a lion throne made of seven precious substances, emitting a light that surpassed the radiance of a hundred thousand suns and moons. Having seen him, they prostrated at his feet and sat to one side. Seated thus, the monks addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: “Noble son, we have now seen you. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied to the monks: “Venerable ones, what you have seen is merely my physical form. If you wish to see my true body, you must cultivate the samādhi of the non-arising of dharmas. The monks asked: “What is the samādhi of the non-arising of dharmas? The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied: “Venerable ones, the samādhi of the non-arising of dharmas is as follows: one should contemplate that all dharmas are originally unborn; one should contemplate that all dharmas are like illusions; one should contemplate that all dharmas are like dreams; one should contemplate that all dharmas are like echoes; one should contemplate that all dharmas are like reflections; one should contemplate that all dharmas are like mirages; one should contemplate that all dharmas are like floating bubbles; one should contemplate that all dharmas are like lightning flashes; one should contemplate that all dharmas are like clouds; one should contemplate that all dharmas are like space. Venerable ones, if you can contemplate all dharmas in this way, you will enter the samādhi of the non-arising of dharmas. Hearing these words, the monks contemplated all dharmas according to the instructions of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and entered the samādhi of the non-arising of dharmas. Having entered this samādhi, they saw that all dharmas were empty, signless, wishless, unarisen, and unceasing. Having seen this, they attained liberation from all suffering and distress. The Buddha told the monks: “Monks, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such inconceivable merit and virtue. Therefore, you should all single-mindedly take refuge in him and pay him homage. When the monks heard the Buddha’s words, they were filled with joy and practiced accordingly. This concludes the Chapter on the Southern Region. [897'] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while traveling through the western region, beheld a great city named Rājagṛha. Within that city lived a king named Bimbisāra. The king had a queen named Vaidehī. The queen gave birth to a son named Ajātaśatru. When the prince grew up, he conspired with Devadatta to plot against his father. One day, King Bimbisāra went out hunting in the forest. The prince, accompanied by a large army, pursued the king. The king fled and entered a mountain cave. The prince and his army searched everywhere but could not find the king. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, out of compassion for the king, manifested as a deer and led the king out of the cave. The prince and his army followed the tracks of the deer and found the king. The prince seized the king and imprisoned him. Queen Vaidehī, hearing that the king had been imprisoned, was overcome with grief and wept. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, knowing her thoughts, manifested as a monk and went to her chamber. Having arrived, he comforted the queen, saying: “Do not grieve, noble lady. If you wish to see the king, you should recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. The queen, hearing these words, single-mindedly recited the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. By the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s majestic spiritual authority, the prison gates opened of their own accord, and the chains binding the king fell away. The king emerged from the prison and went to the queen’s chamber. Having seen the king, the queen was overjoyed. The king then addressed the queen, saying: “Noble lady, you should always recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. The queen, hearing these words, single-mindedly recited the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Subsequently, the prince, fearing the majesty of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, released his father and restored the kingdom to him. The Buddha told the monks: “Monks, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such inconceivable power. Therefore, you should all single-mindedly take refuge in him and pay him homage. When the monks heard the Buddha’s words, they were filled with joy and practiced accordingly. This concludes the Chapter on the Western Region.
